verdict.reasoning: Patient reports shortness of breath for '2, 3 days' and that with walking she 'feel like very short of breath and sometimes I feel like I can't even finish ... a sentence. It's quite difficult to ... complete the talking sometimes.'

Patient reports cough without phlegm or blood ('Have you coughed any phlegm up?... No.' 'Any blood... ? No') but explicitly denies fever when temperature checked: 'Did you say you checked your temperature already?... Was it normal? ... Yeah... What was your temperature? 37.' The doctor interprets 37°C as normal; the patient did not report having a fever of 37°C.

Patient says she 'used to walk to work, but recently I can't' and 'No, I can't' when asked about exercise, showing inability to perform usual exercise. She reports breathlessness 'Just walk' but when asked about stairs: 'are you able to get up and down the stairs? Okay? Doctor: Yeah.'
When asked about asthma: 'Any problems with wheezing when you were a child or any asthma? Doctor: Yes, I had asthma.'
Doctor states 'I also had hay fever' when describing past conditions.
Doctor states 'I also had hay fever and asthma eczema as well.' indicating a history of eczema.

Childhood asthma described as 'It's quite bad.' requiring medication and hospital visits ('Did you have to take medication? Yeah, I take the asthma inhaler.' 'Did you ever have to go to hospital with it? Yeah, sometimes.' 'Did you ever get severely unwell, have to be on intensive care unit ... ? Doctor: No, not that bad.').

Earlier the patient says asthma inhalers stopped 'Few years ago. Like three or four years ago.' but later clarifies current use: 'Do you normally take any asthma inhalers over the last few years? Doctor: Yes... I took sulbutomal... Normally, yeah.' Thus, she did not stop regular inhalers 3–4 years ago; she still uses salbutamol.

Patient indicates ongoing salbutamol use: 'Have you taken any medication? Doctor: I took sulbutomal... Patient: Okay, so you normally take that, do you or is that just recently? Doctor: Normally, yeah.' and frequency 'How often do you normally need it? Doctor: Every few weeks. I'm not sure.' plus with exercise 'what about when you exercise normally, do you have to use medication? Inhalers? Doctor: Yeah.'
When asked 'And do you take any other medications?' patient replies 'No. Nothing else.'
'Any allergies to medications? Doctor: No, no allergies.'
'Do you smoke? Doctor: No, I don't smoke.'
'Do you drink any alcohol regularly? ... Doctor: One glass of wine every... Every two or three days. Depends.'
On who she lives with: 'Do you live on your own or do you live with... Doctor: I live with my partner.'
'And what's your job day to day? Doctor: I'm an engineer.'
Regarding work: 'have you been at work in the last few days? Doctor: No, I can't because I used to walk to work, but recently I work from home or sometimes I take sick leave.'

The transcript: 'Did you say you checked your temperature already? ... Was it normal? ... Yeah... What was your temperature? 37. Yeah.' This indicates 37°C as a normal temperature, not a reported fever.
Chest pain: 'Any chest pain? Doctor: No chest pain? No.' Nocturnal symptoms: 'Have you been woken up at night time at all? Doctor: No. Just daytime walking.'

Clinician’s assessment: 'it sounds like you've had a flare up of your asthma. It could be triggered by if there's more pollen around or... You may have a viral infection causing it to get worse.' This is an acute asthma exacerbation likely triggered by viral illness or allergens.
Patient has chronic hay fever ('I also had hay fever' and 'Any other medical problems? Doctor: I have hay fever as well.') and antihistamine is discussed as ongoing management.

Functional limitation documented: unable to walk to work, cannot exercise ('No, I can't' to exercise), works from home or on sick leave, short of breath with walking and sometimes cannot finish sentences.

'I can prescribe you a peak flow meter so we can check your breathing level, and a spacer to use your inhaler a bit more efficiently, which the pharmacist can show you how you use that when you pick it up.'
'if you increase it so you're taking it two to four puffs, like every four hours initially.' referring to the asthma inhaler (salbutamol).
'the other thing to do would be to take a regular antihistamine, which you can get from the pharmacy. I can put a suggestion on your notes about what to take.'
'when you get the peak flow meter... if you could record a value first thing when you wake up in the evening over the next week.' (interpreted as morning and evening monitoring).

'if you get a high temperature or your wheezing is getting worse, you need to call us back straight away. So we can just advise you further with that.' This is advice for urgent follow-up if fever or wheeze worsens.
'it would be a good idea, when you're feeling better, if we could arrange just a review... You can arrange a review in a week or so... we may need to start some other medications for you.'
'if you get a high temperature or your wheezing is getting worse, you need to call us back straight away.' This is urgent follow-up advice.

'it would be a good idea... if we could arrange just a review... You can arrange a review in a week or so... we may need to start some other medications for you.' describes an asthma review in about a week to assess control and consider further meds.
